languageProof.sectionTitle: What auto-translation gets wrong, and what we get right.
languageProof.intro: Most worksheet sites translate English content with a generic engine and ship the result. Articles end up wrong. Plurals collapse. Accents go missing. Children learn the mistakes. We treat each of our languages as its own catalog — not a translation of English — with vocabulary curated by people who actually teach in that language.

german.heading: German — gender, capitalization, plural irregularity
german.leftAnnotation1: Auto-translation guesses the article from English context. Schule is feminine — no English context tells you that.
german.leftAnnotation2: German nouns are always capitalized. Lowercased nouns teach the wrong rule.
german.leftAnnotation3: The plural is irregular: Schulen, not Schules. Auto-translation regularizes; the correct form is missing.
german.annotation1: die Schule — correct article, every time. Our German vocabulary is keyed to gender, not guessed.
german.annotation2: Schule — capitalized as a German noun should be.
german.annotation3: Schulen — the actual plural, not a Latin-style guess.
german.ariaLabel: Side-by-side comparison: an auto-translated German worksheet with common errors — wrong feminine article ('der' instead of 'die'), uncapitalized noun ('schule' instead of 'Schule'), and English-pluralized form ('schules' instead of 'Schulen') — next to the LessonCraftStudio version with 'die Schule' and 'die Schulen' rendered correctly.

french.heading: French — gender, contractions, accented characters
french.leftAnnotation1: École is feminine, and the article elides before the vowel. Auto-translation does neither.
french.leftAnnotation2: The é isn't decoration — it's part of the word.
french.leftAnnotation3: Preposition + article contract before the vowel: à l'école. Auto-translation leaves them apart.
french.annotation2: à l'école — correct contraction with the preposition.
french.annotation3: Every accent in our French catalog is treated as part of the word.
french.ariaLabel: Side-by-side comparison: an auto-translated French worksheet with common errors — un-elided article ('la école' instead of 'l'école'), un-contracted preposition ('à le école' instead of 'à l'école'), and missing acute accent ('ecole' instead of 'école') — next to the LessonCraftStudio version with 'l'école', 'à l'école', and 'école' rendered correctly.

languageProof.closingLine: Children deserve materials that match the language they're learning. We build to that bar.

topicProse.animals: Animal worksheets are the most useful theme in an early-childhood classroom because the vocabulary travels everywhere. The same friendly cast — cats, cows, birds, fish — turns up across counting and addition, sorting and matching, odd-one-out, and first-letter spelling, so children practise a new skill on pictures they already know and love rather than decoding a fresh context each time. Animal names are also high-frequency in every language we publish, which makes these sheets especially handy when a class has children at different language levels. This page gathers every animal-themed worksheet across the exercise types. Each is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online version and an answer key, and the whole set is available in all 11 languages we publish in.
topicProse.addition: Addition worksheets meet children at the moment adding stops being a counting trick and becomes a fact they can recall. The sheets on this page move along that path: picture-supported sums for the youngest, where a child counts two groups and combines them, through single-digit number sentences, to small two-digit problems for those who are ready. Keeping the format steady lets the thinking stay on the math rather than on figuring out what to do. Each addition worksheet is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online version — the interactive one checks each answer and cheers a clean first pass, the printable is ready for morning work, a maths centre, or homework, and every sheet has an answer key. Pair a picture set with a number-only set to scaffold a lesson, or send one home for five minutes of practice. The whole collection is available in all 11 languages we publish in, so dual-language and international classrooms can give every child addition practice in the language they understand best.
topicProse.subtraction: Subtraction worksheets help children see taking-away as something they can picture before it becomes something they just know. The sheets here start with picture problems — cross out what leaves, count what remains — then move to single-digit number sentences and small two-digit differences as a child grows surer. Because the layout stays consistent, attention goes to the operation rather than to new instructions each time. Each subtraction worksheet is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online activity: the interactive version marks answers immediately and celebrates a clean first pass, while the printable suits guided practice, partner work, or homework, and an answer key is always included. Mix a picture-supported sheet with a number-only one to meet different readiness levels in the same room, or send a sheet home for extra practice. The full set is available in all 11 languages we publish in, so immersion and international classrooms can give every learner subtraction practice in the language they need.
topicProse.alphabet-train: Alphabet train worksheets turn learning the ABCs into something a child can move with their hands. Letter cards ride along the train, and the task is to drag or write each one into the right wagon so the alphabet runs in order — which builds letter recognition, the shape of the sequence, and the left-to-right habit reading depends on. Because the cards are big and picture-clear, a child just meeting these letters, or meeting them in a new language, can take part straight away. Each alphabet train worksheet is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online version: the interactive one snaps cards into place and cheers a finished line, the printable suits a literacy centre or homework, and an answer key is included. The whole set is available in all 11 languages we publish in.
topicProse.wordsearch: Word search worksheets turn early reading into a hunt children actually want to finish. Each puzzle hides a small set of themed words in a grid of letters; a child scans, spots, and drags across each word, matching what they see to the picture clues beside the grid. That scanning is real practice — letter recognition, left-to-right tracking, and locking in new vocabulary — wrapped in a game. The words are short and theme-grouped so the challenge stays right for K-3, and pictures support readers still learning the classroom language. Each word search worksheet is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online version: the interactive one lets children select words right on screen, the printable is ready for early finishers, a literacy centre, or homework, and an answer key is included. The whole set is available in all 11 languages we publish in, so every classroom can build vocabulary in the language its children are learning.
topicProse.matching: Matching worksheets build one of the most useful early skills — seeing how two things go together. A child draws a line from each item on one side to its partner on the other: a picture to its word, a number to a quantity, an object to where it belongs. It is clear, focused practice in association and one-to-one correspondence, and it works across K-3 with picture support throughout. Each matching worksheet is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online version: the interactive one draws the line on a tap-and-tap and marks each pair, the printable suits a centre or homework, and an answer key is included. topicProse.sudoku: Picture sudoku worksheets bring real logic to children long before they can read a rulebook. On a four-by-four grid, a child places friendly pictures so that each row, each column, and each small box holds one of every image — the same deduction grown-up sudoku asks for, scaled to little hands and built from pictures instead of numbers. It is patient, satisfying reasoning practice that builds attention and process-of-elimination thinking, and because it leans on images it works for every child regardless of reading level or home language. Each picture sudoku worksheet is a free printable PDF with a matching play-online version: the interactive one lets children drag pictures into place and checks the finished grid, while the printable suits quiet work, a logic centre, or homework, and an answer key is included.
